strengths: The system combines prior-based LLM selection (retrieval over a unified question bank) with posterior response aggregation (exploration via prior-weighted dropping, exploitation via similarity+perplexity scoring) in a reasonably well-motivated, technically detailed pipeline.

Extensive experiments: main results on 8 benchmarks, scaling curves with increasing LLM count, component ablations, prior-selection retrieval analysis (cross-dataset retrieval patterns), pairwise ranking score comparison to Symbolic-MoE, posterior OCA/MCA diversity analysis, and aggregator-selection study.
The method is designed to be scalable/incremental (new LLMs can be added without retraining a router), addressing a real limitation of prior router-based MACS approaches.
Reasonably thorough hyperparameter and implementation documentation (inference configs, embedding model, sampling parameters) in the appendix, aiding partial reproducibility.
Additional robustness check with extended output-token budget (32k) showing consistent trends.
weaknesses: The central claim ('open-source collaboration beats closed-source LLMs') rests on a fundamentally unequal compute/cost comparison: SMACS issues many LLM calls per query (K=7 referencers × multiple drop-based aggregations × an aggregator LLM, i.e., dozens of forward passes) versus a single call to a closed-source model. No latency, token-cost, or $-cost analysis is provided despite this being central to the paper's framing and to judging whether the 'open-source beats closed-source' narrative is meaningful in practice; this is only briefly acknowledged as a 'limitation' rather than addressed quantitatively.

The comparison against closed-source models is not clearly matched in inference configuration (e.g., whether closed-source baselines used the same custom prompts, temperature, or multiple samples); prompt engineering appears tuned per-benchmark for the proposed pipeline, raising concerns about baseline fairness.

Results appear to come from single runs with stochastic sampling (temperature 0.7) and no reported variance/error bars, which is concerning given LLM output stochasticity and the relatively small test sets for some benchmarks (e.g., AIME has very few questions, making percentage swings like +23% or +63% highly sensitive to a handful of items).

Inconsistent experimental settings undermine claimed rigor: the appendix note that a different aggregator (QwQ-32B instead of Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct) is used for coding tasks in the extended-token experiment, contradicting the 'nearly the same hyperparameters' claim and suggesting some post-hoc tuning per benchmark.

Code is not yet released ('will be released'), and the benchmark test/validation splits are custom (non-standard stratified samples), which combined with unreleased code and question banks limits exact reproducibility.

Individual technical components (RAG-style retrieval for capability estimation, similarity/perplexity-based response scoring, dropout-based ensembling, LLM aggregation) are largely recombinations of existing ideas from RAG, MoA, Self-Consistency, and NAS ranking losses; the novelty is primarily in integration rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The 'open-source upper bound' and 'closed-source upper bound' baselines are per-dataset oracle maxima over different single models, which is a relatively weak/artificial upper bound (not a coherent single system), so exceeding it is a less impressive result than the framing implies.

The paper's title and abstract oversell the practical implication (open-source beats closed-source) without adequately foregrounding that this requires orchestrating 15 models with heavy multi-call inference, which could mislead readers about deployability and cost-effectiveness.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and practically relevant question: whether orchestrating multiple mid-sized open-source LLMs can match or surpass flagship closed-source models.

The proposed two-stage pipeline (retrieval-based prior selection + exploration-exploitation posterior enhancement) is a reasonable, modular combination of existing ideas (RAG-style retrieval, MoA-style aggregation, perplexity/similarity scoring) and is clearly described with formal notation.

Experiments span eight benchmarks across four task categories, include component-wise ablations (Table 2), a scalability study (Fig. 3), and analyses of the retrieval mechanism (Fig. 4) and posterior-enhancement diversity (Fig. 5), which help explain where gains come from.
Appendix experiments on aggregator choice and extended output-token budgets add some robustness checks beyond the main table.
weaknesses: The central claim "open-source collaboration beats closed-source LLMs" compares a 15-model ensemble with multiple inference calls, an aggregator pass, and offline profiling of every model on a large question bank against a single forward pass of a closed-source API; no compute/cost/latency normalization is provided, making the headline comparison fundamentally unfair and the main claim not well supported as stated.

The "unified question bank" used for retrieval-based prior selection is built from validation splits of the very same eight benchmarks used for testing. This undermines the claimed generalization to "diverse" or "unseen" questions and to new domains — the system is essentially doing in-domain nearest-neighbor routing within known benchmark families, which is a much weaker and more narrow claim than advertised in the abstract/intro.

The "open-source/closed-source upper bound" baselines are oracle per-dataset best-model selections (requiring test-time knowledge of which model is best on each dataset), so "exceeding" these oracle baselines by a small margin (+2-3%) is a much less impressive result than the framing suggests, and this is not adequately caveated.

No variance/error bars or repeated-run statistics are reported despite substantial stochasticity in the pipeline (temperature=0.7, prior-dropping sampling, multiple aggregations); some test sets are very small (e.g., AIME has only 30 problems per year), making point-estimate percentage gains potentially within noise.

Reproducibility is incomplete: code is not yet released (placeholder link), several custom dataset splits/sampling procedures are only partially specified, and the method depends on many hand-tuned hyperparameters (K=7, N_sup_base=400, γ=0.95, K_drop=1, n=8, λ=1.0) and benchmark-specific aggregator swaps (e.g., QwQ-32B only for coding tasks in Appendix A.5) that are not well justified or ablated, raising concern about cherry-picking.

The technical novelty is incremental: retrieval-based routing and ensemble aggregation with similarity/perplexity scoring are each well-established ideas (RAG, MoA, self-consistency, LLM-Blender); the contribution is largely a recombination with modest conceptual innovation.

Writing quality issues (typos such as "strengthes", "informations", "vallina", "SMAS", inconsistent labels like "Major Similarity" vs. "MPS") suggest insufficient proofreading, and some notation (e.g., Eq. 6) is sloppy/hard to parse.

The offline cost of profiling all R LLMs on the full question bank (needed before any inference-time benefit) is substantial and not discussed, further obscuring the true cost-benefit tradeoff versus simply querying a strong closed-source model.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across eight diverse benchmarks (math, reasoning, instruction-following, code) with fifteen open-source LLMs and comparison against five closed-source models and six existing collaboration baselines (Symbolic-MoE, MoA, Self-MoA, Self-Consistency, Majority Voting).

The two-stage design (retrieval-based prior LLM selection followed by exploration-exploitation posterior aggregation) is a sensible and reasonably well-motivated combination of ideas from routing/RAG literature and ensemble/best-of-n literature, addressing a real gap (lack of coupling between prior and posterior methods).
Thorough ablation study (Table 2) isolating the contribution of RPS, mean pairwise similarity, PPL, and prior drop, showing each component adds incremental value.

Scaling experiments (Fig. 3) and analysis of retrieval quality (Fig. 4, pairwise ranking score in Table 3) and posterior diversity (Fig. 5, OCA/MCA) provide some mechanistic insight into why the components work, beyond just end task accuracy.

Extensive appendix with dataset splits, LLM bank details, hyperparameters, and prompts supports reproducibility, and an additional experiment with longer output tokens (Table 5) shows the results are not an artifact of a specific token budget.
weaknesses: The central 'open-source beats closed-source' claim is not compute/cost normalized: SMACS invokes up to 7 referencer LLMs plus multiple aggregation calls (n=8) plus a dedicated aggregator per query, versus a single closed-source API call. No latency, token-cost, or FLOP comparison is provided, so the headline claim conflates ensembling with 'open-source superiority' and could equally be read as 'more compute beats less compute,' which is an unsurprising and somewhat expected result rather than a novel finding.

SMACS actually underperforms the closed-source models on GPQA-Diamond and MedMCQA (negative deltas in Table 1), which weakens the strength of the 'consistently beats closed-source' framing used throughout the abstract/intro/title.

No variance/confidence intervals are reported despite stochastic sampling (temperature=0.7) and a resampling-based dropping procedure in EPE; single-run point estimates make it hard to assess whether the reported gains (some as small as ~1-2%) are statistically meaningful.

The technical novelty is incremental: RPS is essentially a k-NN/RAG-style routing scheme similar to prior work already cited (Shnitzer et al. 2023, Chen et al. 2024d, Symbolic-MoE), and EPE's use of perplexity + pairwise similarity for response scoring is a fairly standard combination of existing posterior heuristics; the main contribution is the coupling of the two, which is useful engineering but not conceptually new.

The perplexity-based posterior score computes PPL of the aggregator's own generated aggregation, which can be biased toward shorter/more templated outputs regardless of correctness; no analysis is given to rule out this confound.

The evaluated closed-source models (GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, o3-mini, Claude-3.5/3.7-Sonnet) are already dated relative to current frontier models, and no most-recent flagship (e.g., reasoning-focused or larger context models) is included, limiting the currency/impact of the 'beats closed-source' claim.

Comparisons partly rely on a 'closed/open-source upper bound' defined as the best single-dataset score across models—this is a per-dataset oracle-selection baseline rather than a single deployable system, making the '+2.04%/+2.86%' claims of exceeding this bound somewhat rhetorical rather than a fair systems-level comparison.
Code is only promised ('will be released'), not yet available, so full reproducibility cannot currently be verified despite detailed appendix documentation.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem (scalable multi-LLM collaboration systems that can incorporate new models without retraining) and proposes a coherent two-stage design (retrieval-based prior selection + exploration-exploitation posterior enhancement) that is reasonably well motivated relative to prior router-based and posterior-aggregation methods.

Very extensive experimental campaign: 8 benchmarks spanning math, reasoning, instruction-following, and code; comparisons against 5 closed-source flagships, 15 open-source models, and 6 existing collaboration baselines (Symbolic-MoE, MoA, Self-MoA, Self-Consistency, Majority Voting, Simple Router).

Thorough supplementary analyses: component-wise ablation (Table 10), scaling curves with number of LLMs, cost/latency comparison, aggregator-selection study, perplexity numerical sanity check, 3-seed statistical stability check on a subset of datasets, and multiple out-of-distribution robustness experiments (single-dataset question bank, and entirely new external benchmarks such as HumanEval/FinQA/LiveMathBench).

Reasonably detailed method formalization (capability vectors, retrieval weighting, prior-driven dropout sampling, hybrid posterior scoring) and thorough appendix with implementation/hyperparameter details and prompts, aiding partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The prominent claim of 'exceeding the open-source upper bound' is based on the best single model *per dataset* rather than a true upper bound achievable by any one model on all tasks; this terminology overstates what is actually a comparison against a virtual oracle ensemble, and could mislead readers about the significance of the result.

The unified question bank is constructed largely from validation splits of the very benchmarks used for evaluation (AIME, MATH, MMLU-PRO, GPQA, MedMCQA, IFEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench), so the prior-selection mechanism benefits from strong in-distribution similarity between question-bank and test questions; while OOD ablations partially address this, the main results likely benefit from this favorable setup and the paper does not fully disentangle in-distribution retrieval benefit from genuine cross-task generalization.

Several benchmarks used for headline claims (notably AIME2024 with ~30 items) have very small test sets, so reported percentage-point gains (e.g., +5.36% vs GPT-4.1) can correspond to only one or two additional correct answers; the paper does not report confidence intervals or variance for the main results table, limiting confidence in the precision of the claimed improvements (the later 3-seed analysis only covers 4 of 8 datasets).

No functioning code link is provided in the manuscript ('The code is released at' with no URL), which is a meaningful reproducibility gap for a paper whose core contribution is a fairly complex multi-stage system with numerous hyperparameters (K, Nsup_base, γ, Kdrop, n, λ).

The individual technical components (RAG-style retrieval for capability estimation, best-of-n/self-consistency style multiple aggregation, perplexity- and similarity-based reranking) are largely recombinations of existing techniques; the novelty lies mainly in their integration rather than in a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

The aggregator model is fixed (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct) across all tasks and settings, which is somewhat in tension with the paper's framing of full instance-level adaptivity and scalability, and the choice appears to be selected via test-set-informed comparison (Appendix A.4) rather than a principled, task-agnostic criterion.

Comparisons to baselines vary in the compute/model budget they are allotted (e.g., Self-MoA/Self-Consistency use a single best model with 8 samples vs. SMCS's 15-model pool with multiple referencers and aggregations); although cost/latency figures are reported, a more careful compute-matched comparison would strengthen the fairness of the comparison.

strengths: The paper presents extensive empirical evaluation across eight diverse benchmarks and includes multiple auxiliary analyses (scalability curves, OOD retrieval, aggregator selection, perplexity numerical analysis, cost/latency, and repeated-seed statistical variance), which shows an unusually thorough experimental effort for an ensemble/routing-style paper.

The framing of unifying prior LLM-selection with posterior response-enhancement into a single pipeline is a reasonable and coherent systems-level contribution, addressing a real practical pain point (scalability when adding new LLMs) that prior routing/MoE literature does not fully solve.

The retrieval-based prior selection mechanism is simple to implement (no per-LLM router training) and the ablation study (Table 10) does show incremental gains from each component, lending some support to the internal validity of the design choices.
Cost and latency reporting, together with a hyperparameter-vs-cost sensitivity study (Tables 11-13), is a nice practical addition that many multi-agent papers omit.
weaknesses: A central soundness concern: the unified question bank used to compute each LLM's 'prior' capability vector is built by combining the validation splits of the exact same eight benchmarks the system is tested on. This gives SMCS strong benchmark-specific and near-in-distribution information that none of the closed-source baselines (GPT-4.1, GPT-o3-mini, Claude) receive, making the headline comparisons (SMCS vs. flagship closed-source LLMs) not apples-to-apples; the reported '+5.36% over GPT-4.1' framing overstates a fair generalization claim.

The 'exploration-exploitation' terminology is largely rhetorical: the actual mechanism is a softmax-weighted random dropping of references followed by repeated aggregation and hybrid scoring (similarity + perplexity) — a relabeled combination of existing self-consistency/best-of-n/MoA ideas, without a rigorous exploration-exploitation (e.g., bandit-theoretic) formulation or regret/optimality argument to justify the name.

Novelty is incremental: RPS is essentially a kNN/RAG-style capability lookup similar to existing cluster-based or embedding-based routers already discussed in related work (e.g., Jitkrittum et al., Srivatsa et al.), and EPE recombines well-known techniques (dropout-style sampling, LLM aggregation à la MoA, perplexity/self-consistency filtering) rather than introducing a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

Using perplexity as a posterior quality signal is questionable for reasoning-heavy tasks (math, code) where fluency does not track correctness; the post-hoc 'numerical analysis' justifying its scale compatibility with the similarity score is not a substitute for validating that PPL actually correlates with correctness on these specific tasks.

The system has many hand-tuned hyperparameters (K=7, Nsup_base=400, γ=0.95, Kdrop=1, n=8, λ=1.0, choice of Llama-3.3-70B as aggregator) that appear selected via extensive search on the same benchmarks used for final reporting, raising overfitting/benchmark-tuning concerns and limiting confidence in generalization to unseen tasks/LLMs despite the OOD experiments.

The 'code is released at' link is blank in the manuscript, and several implementation details (e.g., exact cost computation methodology, how closed-source API costs vs. open-source hosting costs are equated in Table 2) are underspecified, hurting reproducibility.

Comparisons to baselines like Self-MoA, Self-Consistency, and Majority Voting appear to use only the single best LLM (or default configurations) rather than being tuned as thoroughly as SMCS, which could bias the comparison in SMCS's favor.

Statistical robustness is limited: only 3 seeds on 4 of 8 datasets are reported for variance, and no significance testing (e.g., paired tests) is provided against the strongest baselines despite small margins in several cells (e.g., GPQA-Diamond, IFEval) where SMCS underperforms or ties baselines.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across 8 diverse benchmarks (math, code, reasoning, instruction-following, medical QA) with comparisons to closed-source LLMs, 15 open-source LLMs, and several collaboration baselines (MoA, Self-MoA, Symbolic-MoE, Self-Consistency, Majority Voting).

Thorough ablation studies: component-wise ablation (RPS, similarity score, PPL, prior drop), aggregator selection analysis, scalability curves with increasing LLM count, and cost/latency analysis showing the method is not merely a brute-force compute increase.

Good reproducibility practices: detailed hyperparameters, LLM bank composition, prompts for every benchmark, and statistical significance testing with multiple seeds (mean ± std) on a subset of datasets.

The retrieval-based prior selection is a sensible, largely training-free mechanism for capability estimation that can plausibly scale to new LLMs without retraining a router, addressing a real limitation of prior router-based MCS methods.
Additional robustness checks (OOD question banks, extended output-token budgets, perplexity numerical analysis) strengthen confidence in the practical validity of the design choices.
weaknesses: Many router-based baselines discussed at length in Related Work (Zooter, RouterDC, GraphRouter, MODEL-SAT, Shnitzer et al.) are never empirically compared against; only Symbolic-MoE is benchmarked, leaving the claimed advantages over the broader prior-selection literature largely unverified.

The capability profiling (question bank) is built from validation splits of the very same benchmark distributions used for testing, which is a favorable setup for the retrieval mechanism; the OOD experiments only partially address whether this generalizes to genuinely novel, unseen task distributions in deployment.

The headline comparisons against single closed-source models (e.g., '+5.36% vs GPT-4.1') combine 15 collaborating models against one model; while cost/latency are reported to partially justify this, the framing as 'surpassing GPT-4.1' could overstate the significance of an inherently favorable many-vs-one comparison.

The method presupposes access to verifiable ground-truth labels for building LLM capability vectors (Eq. 1) and evaluating correctness; this limits applicability to tasks with exact-match or otherwise easily verifiable answers, and this limitation is not clearly discussed.

Claims of 'scalability' are not fully substantiated with respect to the cost of profiling new LLMs on the full question bank when integrating them, which itself could become a bottleneck as the LLM pool grows.

Some design choices (threshold coefficient γ, base retrieval number, λ balance coefficient) appear to be tuned heuristically without deeper theoretical or sensitivity justification beyond the cost/accuracy curves in the appendix.

The novelty is somewhat incremental, combining known ideas (RAG-style nearest-neighbor retrieval for routing, ensemble aggregation with dropout-based diversity, hybrid PPL/similarity scoring) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism.
